items.note: Plain 'what,' distinct from なんの (nan no) 'what kind of' seen with なんじ (nanji, 'what time') and なんにん (nannin, 'how many people') — なに (nani) alone asks about an unspecified thing, as in なにをしますか (nani o shimasu ka), 'what will you do?'

items.note: Follows the general [noun] + を (o) + します (shimasu) pattern from テニスをします (tenisu o shimasu, 'play tennis') and しごとをします (shigoto o shimasu, 'work') this lesson — します supplies 'do,' the noun supplies the activity.

しごと (shigoto, 'work') is the same noun from Lesson 3's しごとはくじからごじまでです (shigoto wa kuji kara goji made desu, 'work is from 9:00 to 5:00'); here it combines with を (o) + します (shimasu) to form the verb 'to work'.

items.note: Attaches to a number to count people: さんにん (san-nin, 'three people'), ごにん (go-nin, 'five people'). One and two break the pattern completely — ひとり (hitori) and ふたり (futari) — and four uses よ (yo) rather than よん (yon): よにん (yo-nin).
items.reviewNote: Written 〜にん in the source.

items.note: なん (nan, 'how many') + the counter にん (nin, '…people'). Restaurant and hotel staff ask a customer the same question with the polite なんめいさまですか (nanmeisama desu ka) — see that card.

items.note: The polite form of this lesson's なんにん (nan-nin, 'how many people') — the book glosses it exactly that way. めいさま (meisama) is an honorific counter for people you are serving, so staff use it about YOU and you never use it about your own group. Answer with the plain counter: ふたりです (futari desu), 'two people.'

items.note: A more formal です (desu), heard from shop or business staff — compare ございます (gozaimasu) inside ありがとうございます (arigatou gozaimasu) from Frequently Used Expressions, a related but different polite form.
items.reviewNote: Written 〜でございます in the source.

items.note: でございます (degozaimasu) in use: a business naming itself on the phone. てんまさ (Tenmasa) is the tempura restaurant in this lesson's dialogue. The everyday form would be てんまさです (tenmasa desu) — でございます (degozaimasu) is what staff say to a customer.
items.reviewNote: From this lesson's Speaking Practice dialogue — the only place the chapter actually uses でございます.
items.target: てんまさでございます

items.english: This is the Nozomi Department Store.
items.note: The same でございます (degozaimasu) pattern as てんまさでございます (tenmasa de gozaimasu), with のぞみデパート (Nozomi Depaato) from Lesson 1 — any business names itself this way when it picks up the phone.
items.reviewNote: AI-suggested: a second worked example of でございます built from vocabulary already introduced (のぞみデパート, Lesson 1), so the pattern generalizes beyond the one fictitious restaurant name.
items.target: のぞみデパートでございます

items.note: The affirmative of Lesson 2's わかりません (wakarimasen, 'I don't know') — one verb, opposite polarity. Japanese reaches for it where English would say 'know' as well as 'understand'.
items.reviewNote: Possibly premature — explicitly taught later in Lesson 24: Work and Interests: I Work for an Apparel Maker (explicitly re-taught as a dedicated vocabulary-table row and a Key Sentence entry)

items.note: Past form of わかります (wakarimasu, 'understand, see, get it'). Japanese answers in the PAST tense at the moment of understanding where English uses the present — say わかりました (wakarimashita), not わかります, for 'got it'.
お (o, honorific prefix) + なまえ (namae, 'name') from Lesson 2 — same pattern as おくに (okuni, 'your country') and おでんわばんごう (odenwa bangou) below: always someone else's, never your own.
